meta.title: Who really said "Poetry is music written for the human voice"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Maya Angelou said it on PBS in 1982 — but credited her Stamps, Arkansas mentor Bertha Flowers. Quote Investigator credits Flowers, not Angelou.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Poetry is music written for the human voice'?
meta.ogDescription: Angelou spoke the line on Bill Moyers' Creativity in 1982 — and credited Mrs. Bertha Flowers, the teacher who gave her back her voice.

answer.label: Not Maya Angelou — actually Bertha Flowers
answer.authorDates: Educator in Stamps, Arkansas · Maya Angelou’s childhood mentor
answer.sourceLine: Angelou really did say these words — on camera, in the episode “A Portrait of Maya Angelou” of Bill Moyers’ PBS series Creativity, broadcast 8 January 1982 — but she said them as a quotation of Mrs. Bertha Flowers, the Stamps, Arkansas woman who coaxed her out of years of silence. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the line should be credited to Flowers, with Angelou as the person who popularized it.

source.excerpt: So, she read to me and then she told me that poetry was music written for the human voice. She must have told me that 50 times.
trail: 1969 — I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings introduces Mrs. Bertha Flowers and her teaching that it takes the human voice to infuse words with deeper meaning, but not this aphorism, per Quote Investigator’s check against scans of chapter 15 ↗.

8 January 1982 — the Creativity episode “A Portrait of Maya Angelou” airs on PBS; the transcript at BillMoyers.com ↗ has Angelou saying Mrs. Flowers told her poetry was music written for the human voice, fifty times over. Reviews in the Chicago Tribune and Los Angeles Times that same day both reprint the remark, crediting Flowers.

11 December 1983 — Angelou repeats the saying in a Charlotte Observer interview, adding that until you read it aloud you will never love it; the interview was reprinted in Conversations with Maya Angelou ↗ (University Press of Mississippi, 1989), spreading it further.
2001 — Random House Webster’s Quotationary files it correctly, under MRS. FLOWERS, quoted by Maya Angelou — as Quote Investigator ↗ records. The quote sites that followed dropped Flowers entirely.
source.excerptNote: Maya Angelou, describing Mrs. Flowers in the Creativity episode transcript published by BillMoyers.com. The transcript renders the saying as reported speech; the same-day Chicago Tribune review of the broadcast, quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, printed it as a direct quotation in the familiar present-tense form.

source.rightsNote: Every documented appearance of this line is 1982 or later: the PBS Creativity broadcast and transcript of 8 January 1982, the newspaper reviews published that same day, and the 11 December 1983 Charlotte Observer interview reprinted in Conversations with Maya Angelou (University Press of Mississippi, 1989). Those works are in copyright, and no pre-1931 printing of the sentence is known, so nothing here is public domain.

author.name: Bertha Flowers
author.heading: Who was Mrs. Flowers?
author.metaLine: Educator in Stamps, Arkansas · Maya Angelou’s childhood mentor
author.bio: In I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969) Angelou introduces her as Mrs. Bertha Flowers, “the aristocrat of Black Stamps” — the well-to-do neighbour who invited a mute eight-year-old to her cool, shaded house, fed her tea cookies, read A Tale of Two Cities aloud to her and sent her home with poems to memorize and recite. Flowers’ teaching was that words are incomplete on the page: it takes the human voice to give them their deeper meaning. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas documents the Stamps educator who mentored the young Angelou — reading and discussing classical literature with her, and credited by Angelou with helping her reclaim her voice — under the name Beulah Lee Sampson Flowers (1883–1965).

misattribution.heading: How Angelou ended up owning it
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reliably mis-credited things Maya Angelou ever said out loud — precisely because she really did say it, on national television, just never as her own.

items.why: Quote mills print the sentence under Angelou’s name with Bertha Flowers nowhere in sight. AZQuotes ↗ credits Angelou and sources it to a 1989 PBS program, The Power of the Word — not the Creativity broadcast of January 1982 that Quote Investigator ↗ documents.

A longer variant beginning “Poetry is music for the human voice…” — dropping written and continuing into a second sentence about a poem not coming into its own until it is spoken — circulates on Goodreads ↗ under Angelou’s name with no source named, on a page that carries Goodreads’ own warning that community-added quotes are unverified.

items.who: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
items.why: It is natural to look for the aphorism in Angelou’s 1969 memoir, where Mrs. Flowers appears at length. It is not there. Quote Investigator ↗, checking chapter 15 against scans, finds a related but different remark from Flowers — that it takes the human voice to infuse words with the shades of deeper meaning — and an instruction to memorize a poem and recite it.

misattribution.truthLine: Angelou said the words on camera and in print, and in every documented instance she handed the credit away rather than taking it — “she must have told me that 50 times.” Quote Investigator ↗ credits Bertha Flowers.

context.heading: Why this one matters
lead: Angelou stopped speaking at seven and a half. She had been raped in St. Louis, the man who did it was killed after she named him, and she concluded that her voice had killed him — so she put it away. The woman who gave it back was Mrs. Flowers, whom Angelou called the lady of Stamps: she invited the silent child to her house, read A Tale of Two Cities aloud to her, told her that poetry was music written for the human voice, and asked her to go home and say a poem out loud. Angelou practised under her grandmother’s high bed. In the Moyers transcript ↗ she puts the result in one line: “Mrs. Flowers gave me back my voice.”

That is why the sentence is a poetics rather than a platitude. It claims a poem is unfinished until somebody speaks it — the principle Angelou then built a career on, writing verse meant to be heard rather than scanned. Wikipedia’s survey of her poetry ↗ records that she wrote poems so that they would be read aloud, and that critics find them most alive in her own delivery.
context.detailsSummary: Two loose ends: her name, and a date that doesn’t match
detailsBody: The name. Angelou’s memoir and every quotation source call her Mrs. Bertha Flowers. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas ↗ entry for the Stamps educator who mentored the young Angelou — who read and discussed classical literature with her, and whom Angelou credited with helping her reclaim her voice and self-confidence — is filed under Beulah Lee Sampson Flowers (1883–1965), an educator, community leader, political activist and businesswoman.

The date. Random House Webster’s Quotationary (2001) files the line under MRS. FLOWERS, quoted by Maya Angelou, and cites a Bill Moyers interview in the Creativity television series dated 24 February 1992 — as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The episode transcript published by BillMoyers.com ↗ is dated 8 January 1982, the same date as the two newspaper reviews Quote Investigator cites.
